DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The valuation Band was confirmed in Band B with effect from 1 April 1993. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal has been brought in respect of 171 Church Street, Ripley DE5 9TE. A proposal 
was served on the Listing Officer by the appellant, in dispute of the Band B assessment and 
seeking a reduction to Band A. The Listing Officer reviewed the Band and, on 14 January 
2026, issued a decision notice confirming the property in Band B with effect from 1 April 
1993. 
 
4. 
In this appeal, the relevant date for consideration of the physical state of the dwelling and its 
locality was 1 April 1993, the date the subject property entered the valuation list 
 
5. 
Prior to this hearing the appellant had requested that this matter be heard in her absence 
based on the evidence provided. 
 
6. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. 
On her appeal form the appellant stated as follows: 
 
“The listing officer compared my property 171 Church street with 102 and 100a Church 
street, these are not comparable properties 102 and 100a are much newer properties with 
Garages and may not have existed in 1993. My property is no different to 167 Church Street, 
which adjoins the same block of as 171 with 169 in between. 167 and 171 are identical 
properties, both having later building additions. 171 has a slightly larger entrance to the side 
of the property that 167 but they have very similar size plots of land, 167 also has a parking 
space to the front of the property, I do not agree that 171 is a band B if 167 is a band A. they 
are basically the same 2 up 2 down property built at the same time.  
Therefore 171 is not comparable with 100a but is comparable with 167 so I would appreciate 
this being reassessed and do not accept the listing officer’s decision.” 
 
8. 
The subject property is an end terraced house built pre-1919. Within the 93m2 reduced 
covered area (RCA), there are three bedrooms, two bathrooms, one reception room and a 
kitchen. The property also benefits from a conservatory and off street parking. 
 
9. 
For council tax purposes, domestic dwellings are measured to RCA. In brief, this is the area 
of a building measured externally at each floor level and includes perimeter wall thickness, 
external projections (such as a bay), and areas occupied by internal walls, partitions and 
stairwells. Measurements are done in this way to give uniformity and fairness and facilitates 
easy comparison between dwellings. Loft conversions with sloping ceilings are calculated on 
external areas any internal areas with a head height of below 1.5m2 are excluded. 
Additionally, garages are excluded from the RCA.

Relevant Law 
 
10. The panel had regard to the legislation for council tax and, in particular, the Council Tax 
(Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992, which amongst other things, 
required that the value of a domestic property for council tax Banding purposes was the 
amount which it might reasonably have been expected to realise had it been sold on the 
open market by a willing vendor on the antecedent valuation day (AVD) 1 April 1991. 
 
11. Under regulation 6 of the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 
1992 (SI 1992 No. 550), each valuation Band represents a value that a dwelling might 
reasonably have been expected to realise. The Bands are set out in section 5(2) of the Local 
Government Finance Act 1992, with the relevant Bands in relation to this appeal being:   
 
Band A – values not exceeding £40,000; and 
Band B – values exceeding £40,000 but not exceeding £52,000. 
 
Discussion 
 
12. Therefore, regardless of whether a property existed on 1 April 1991, or was purchased at a 
later date, in order to allow fairness and uniformity between all council tax valuations, all 
domestic property must be valued at the common date of 1 April 1991 and the level of value 
on that date, albeit within a range of values, had to be determined. 
 
13. Band A represents properties with a range of values not exceeding £40,000 as at 1 April 
1991; therefore, for the appeal to be successful and the Band to be reduced it must be 
shown that the subject property would have sold for less than £40,000 on 1 April 1991 
 
14. The best evidence on which to determine the Band of a property was therefore considered to 
be an open market sale of either the subject property, or of ones which are comparable with 
it, that had completed on or close to the valuation date of 1 April 1991. 
 
15. The Listing Officer had provided sales evidence for four properties which, Mrs Fisher 
submitted, were comparable and supported Band B for the subject property. In particular the 
panel noted that: 152, Nottingham Road, Ripley, was a two bedroom, one bathroom end-
terraced house with an RCA of 65m2, it had sold for £38,500 on 15 May 1991; 60, Pease Hill 
Road, Ripley, was a two bedroom, one bathroom end-terraced house with an RCA of 61m2, it 
had sold for £39,950 on 26 April 1991; and 103, Pentrich Road, Ripley, was a two bedroom 
one bathroom end-terraced house with an RCA of 73m2 it had sold for £37,500 on 26 April 
1991. The panel found this evidence to be of some significance, it noted that these properties 
were of notably smaller than the subject property and had sold very close to the AVD, it 
determined that these sales supported Band B for the subject property which was in the 
same location and had an RCA of 93m2 which included a third bedroom and a second 
bathroom.  
 
16. The panel determined that had the subject property been placed for sale on the open market 
on 1 April 1991 it would probably have achieved a sales value above the lower band B 
threshold. 
 
17. The panel was aware that a property’s Banding could be determined by tone, should the 
‘tone of the list’ have been established. A tone of value/Band is established when a number 
of properties, similar in size, character, quality, detachment and location were attributed the 
same level of assessment/Band which, over time, had not been challenged. Assessments

that had been challenged and subsequently agreed by parties or determined by a Tribunal 
panel were also instrumental in establishing the tone. Mrs Fisher referred to 12, Pit Lane, 
Waingroves, Ripley, and 61, Queen Street, Waingroves, Ripley, which were also three-
bedroom terraced houses with two bathrooms, they RCA’s of 108m2 and 102m2 respectively 
and were all in Band B. 
 
18. The panel noted that these properties were larger than the subject property and that 12, Pit 
Lane, had a garage, however, it was aware that band B comprised a wide bandwidth, which 
included properties with capital values as at 1 April 1991 levels exceeding £40,000 but not 
exceeding £52,000. As such, the panel held that band B was large enough to encompass a 
range of property types and sizes. Furthermore, the panel identified that the subject property 
had been ascribed Band B since the valuation list was compiled and there appeared to be a 
settled tone of Banding in the road. As the valuation list had been in force for over 30 years, 
the panel found that the tone should only be disturbed when there is strong evidence to do 
so. 
 
19. The panel turned to the evidence submitted by the appellant including 167, 169 and 173 
Church Street in Waingroves. The panel noted that these properties were smaller than the 
subject property when they were ascribed band A. The appellant had also referred to four 
properties which appeared to be larger than the subject property and in band A. The panel 
was aware that three of the four properties were marked to be reviewed it was aware that the 
banding of similar properties can appear inconsistent for the following reasons:  
 
• Properties which had been extended but not yet sold. The Listing Officer is 
unable to review the Band of an extended/improved property until there has 
been a relevant transaction, e.g., a sale. 
• Properties that had been extended and subsequently sold but not yet 
reviewed. The Listing Officer relies upon reports from the Billing Authority to 
notify any changes to a property 
 
20. The appellant had referred to the Nationwide House Price Index and sales of the subject 
property in 2014 and 2025. The panel viewed the calculations with caution as it was aware 
that house price calculators and indices were by their very nature unreliable for council tax 
purposes and, therefore, of little assistance, as they covered a wide geographic area, which 
contained great variation between different localities and included different types of 
properties. For the purposes of this particular appeal, the panel was solely concerned with 
terraced houses in the immediate vicinity and sales close to the AVD, house price 
calculators/indices did not provide the level of detail required. The panel, therefore, attached 
little weight to this evidence.  
 
21. The appellant had also referred to four Energy Performance Certificates to demonstrate the 
size of various properties, unfortunately the panel was aware that these certificates do not 
reflect the method of measuring used for council tax which is out lined in paragraph nine 
above. 
 
22. In appeals of this nature, the legal burden of proof rests upon the appellant to show that the 
current Band is incorrect. Considering the evidence before it, the panel held that insufficient 
evidence had been provided to demonstrate that the Band B assessment was excessive. 
 
Conclusion

23. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the appeal was dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
24. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
25. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.
